newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi faces crunch vote on Albania force.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi faces crunch vote on Albania force.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, his fragile alliance facing the toughest test of its 11 months in office, searched for a last-minute political deal to back the deployment of a security force for Albania.

The Chamber of Deputies (lower house) was due to vote on the Italian-led mission on Wednesday. The centre-left could be forced into the humiliating position of having to support an opposition motion after the desertion of its hard-left ally.
Prodi comfortably won a first vote on Tuesday in the upper Senate, where he has a majority, despite a vote against the government resolution from the opposition Freedom Alliance.

Centre-right leader Silvio Berlusconi suggested his bloc could vote "no" again, posing a dangerous dilemma for Prodi after the Communist Refoundation party, whose support he depends on for a majority in the Chamber, refused its backing.
"Nothing has changed for us after the Senate vote. We'll go on with the decisions we have taken," Berlusconi told reporters.
"If they want the mission to leave, the only way is to vote for our resolution. If they don't, it will be their fault if the mission doesn't leave," he said.
Prodi met his centre-left allies late on Tuesday to discuss a face-saving deal that would ensure that the U.N.-approved force, the first to be led by Italy, is deployed as planned next week.
Greens Party spokesman Luigi Manconi told reporters after the meeting that the coalition would not vote for the Freedom Alliance motion in Wednesday's vote.
"There's still time to work out a consensus motion with the Freedom Alliance," Fabio Mussi, leader of the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left in the Chamber, said earlier.
"There's no need for despair."
Parliamentary sources said Prodi had appealed to Berlusconi in a telephone call on Tuesday afternoon to support the government in the vote in the Chamber.
The Freedom Alliance planned to meet at 10.30 a.m. (0830 GMT) on Wednesday to discuss its stance. The debate in the Chamber is scheduled to begin at midday (1000 GMT).
Prodi, well aware that Italy's international credibility is at stake over the mission, has appealed for all-party support.

The Freedom Alliance had planned to back Prodi but abruptly changed tack after a junior foreign minister, Piero Fassino, caused a diplomatic storm when he said the government believed Albania's rightist President Sali Berisha should leave office.

Albania responded with outrage in two strongly-worded demands for clarification. Prodi quickly distanced himself from the remarks and wrote to Berisha and Prime Minister Bashkim Fino assuring them Italy would not meddle in Albanian affairs.
Relations had already been strained by the sinking last month of a boat packed with refugees after it collided with an Italian navy ship escorting it back to port. Tirana says more than 80 died.

That incident sparked Refoundation's split with the government and brought to a head almost a year of tension with the hard-left party on virtually every subject, from privatisation to welfare reform to the European single currency.

Cesare Salvi, leftist leader in the Senate, told reporters that Refoundation was "making a big mistake this time" and that the government would have to take a long, hard look at "the reasons for staying together" after the Chamber vote.

Italy has also run into trouble with Greece over how the force, to which Italy is expected to contribute 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Romania 400 and Spain 300, will be deployed in the lawless Balkan state.
Austria and Denmark are also considering joining the mission, which will protect aid shipments to Albania following violence last month after the failure of shady savings schemes.
